features.description: Two giant lobes of GeV gamma rays discovered in Fermi-LAT maps, symmetric about the Galactic plane and rooted at the Galactic centre, with sharp edges and a hard spectrum. They are probably the product of a burst of activity of the central black hole or of nuclear star formation within the last ~10 Myr. Invisible to the eye: they are seen in gamma rays (and, closer to the plane, in the microwave 'haze'). Label at the centre of the northern lobe. Shape: each lobe reaches from the plane to latitude 50 deg, i.e. 8178 pc × tan 50° above Sgr A* when its far edge is taken in the plane of the sky through the centre, so the lobe centre is 4873 pc above (below) Sgr A*; the 40 deg width at the lobe-centre distance gives the cross-section; the extent along the line of sight is not measured and is set equal to the width. Semi-axes (line of sight × across × vertical) 3465 × 3465 × 4873 pc, approximate.

features.description: Two enormous shells of soft X-ray emission (0.6-1.0 keV) found in the first all-sky survey of the eROSITA telescope, about twice the size of the Fermi bubbles which they enclose; the northern one includes the long-known North Polar Spur / Loop I region. Predehl et al. 2020 interpret them as a shock driven into the Galaxy's hot halo by an energy release at the Galactic centre some tens of millions of years ago. Invisible to the eye: they are seen only in X-rays. Label at the centre of the northern lobe. Shape: Predehl et al. 2020 describe each bubble as a (quasi-)spherical thick shell with an outer diameter of 14 kpc, reaching about 14 kpc above (below) the plane; each lobe is drawn as a sphere of radius 7 kpc centred 7000 pc above (below) Sgr A*. Semi-axes 7000 × 7000 × 7000 pc, approximate.
